results.title: Doubles basic
results.creator_credit: Bill Mason, Bill Brind, Colin Low and National Film Board of Canada
results.brief_description:
Episode of Series “Path of the Paddle”.
Paddling double, the canoeists demonstrate the basic paddling strokes and how to apply them in a variety of combinations to move the canoe at will. Throughout the film the application of each stroke in rapids is shown briefly, with emphasis on the necessity of working as a well-coordinated team.

results.title: Word problems 2: variables
results.creator_credit: Mark M Williams, Bill Hanlon and KLVX (Television station : Las Vegas, Nev.)
results.brief_description:
Episode of Series “Algebra, you can do it”.
This program shows how to write word problems with two variables in a mathematical way and how then to solve these equations by linear combination or substitution. Suitable for lower to middle secondary level students. A guide accompanies this video.

results.title: Something to sing about
results.creator_credit: Martin Daley, Marguerite Grey, ABC-TV (Australia), AFFC and Something to Sing About
results.brief_description: The Sydney Gay and Lesbian Choir has a repertoire which ranges from Gershwin to madrigals, spirituals to ABBA. The choir represents a positive force within the community; not just on the gay scene but across contemporary Australia. This documentary focuses on the choir’s defence of their National Choral Championship and is an uplifting and moving experience.

results.title: Tuvalu
results.creator_credit: Denmark, Leif Stubkjaer, and U-V Film and Video
results.brief_description:
Episode of Series “Oceans of Dreams - Currents of Change Series”.
Tuvalu has no rivers, no natural forests, scant soil cover and at its highest point is only 5 metres above sea level. The film looks at contemporary Tuvalu, the old ways, the new challenges and how people live.

results.title: Solo basic
results.creator_credit: Bill Mason, Bill Brind and National Film Board of Canada
results.brief_description:
Episode of Series “Path of the Paddle”.
The joy and poetry of paddling solo are illustrated in this film, as are all the basic strokes used in maintaining complete control of the canoe. With the aid of animated lines, the path of the paddle is clearly defined so there can be no mistaking what the paddle is doing. The use of the various strokes in rapids is demonstrated sufficiently to whet the appetite to move on.

results.title: Niue
results.brief_description:
Episode of Series “Oceans of Dreams - Currents of Change Series”.
Niue is the world’s largest coral atoll and the world’s smallest nation. A New Zealand protectorate from 1901 until 1974, Niue is now self-governing. All Niueans are New Zealand citizens and this has encouraged a trend in depopulation; 10,000 Niueans live in New Zealand, 2,300 live on Niue itself. The island enjoys a high standard of living but is isolated through poor transport and communication links. It also has the problems of a tiny economic base, and trying to retain a cultural identity. The film examines the contemporary issues and challenges facing Niue and its people.

results.title: Solo whitewater
results.creator_credit: Bill Mason, Bill Brind and National Film Board of Canada
results.brief_description:
Episode of Series “Path of the Paddle”.
This film explains clearly how to locate a deep water channel by reading the rapids and how to apply the many paddling strokes and manoeuvres to steer the canoe where you want it to go. It also depicts what happens if you make a mistake and “wipe out” in a turbulent rapid, and how to survive the swim. (Award: Venissieux.)

results.title: Doubles whitewater
results.creator_credit: Bill Mason, Bill Brind, Colin Low and National Film Board of Canada
results.brief_description:
Episode of Series “Path of the Paddle”.
Running rapids will always be a calculated risk. But risk diminishes with skill and knowledge. In this film, two canoeists paddling double demonstrate how to read the rapids, plan a course and follow it in complete control of the boat, using the basic paddling strokes. The strokes can be used in endless combination to reduce the risk of whitewater canoeing and increase the sheer joy and exuberance of a whitewater run.
